evidence.note: CONFIRMED: the claim 'merge --force --approval spends the single-use approval before git runs' was refuted-able via a regression test; test_a_failed_git_landing_does_not_spend_the_approval failed on unfixed code (assert _asks[ask].used == 0 saw 1) and passes after deferring the spend to post-landing.
Read governing rules for merge force + approvals (r-gemini-key-load, r-task-phase-needs-wave) and the consume/approvals sites; the fix follows the single-use digest-bound approval contract.
Split approval check (consume.check, no spend) from spend; merge_force.authorise validates only; merge spends via merge_force.spend after W.merge lands.

chunk_findings.detail: `check` performs only a non-reserving read: two interleaved callers with the same single-use `ask_id` can both get `Decision.ok` before either `spend` records `ask.consumed`. Both callers may then perform their guarded side effect; the first `spend` consumes the approval and the second `spend` fails only after its side effect has already happened, defeating the single-use guarantee. The old `spend` checked and recorded under one `log.transaction()` and would have refused the losing caller before the side effect.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

chunk_findings.detail: `spend` returns `CN.spend(log, canon_of(log, item, a), approval).stamp` without checking the result’s `ok`/`message` fields, even though `authorise` immediately above treats `CN.check` as a fallible result. Because `authorise` no longer consumes the approval before landing, `spend` is the point that must still enforce the single-use guarantee. A concrete interleaving: two concurrent `merge --force --approval A` invocations on different worktrees both pass `CN.check` while `A` is unused, both git landings succeed, and the first `CN.spend` consumes `A`. The second `CN.spend` now sees an already-consumed approval and returns a non-ok result, but this function still returns its `.stamp` (typically `None`) instead of propagating the refusal. The second merge is then recorded as forced with no valid single-use approval, or the caller emits a `merge.forced` event with a bogus proof.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/merge_force.py:spend

chunk_findings.detail: `check` validates a single-use approval with no lock and no reservation, and `spend` only appends `ask.consumed` later. Two callers that share one `ask_id` and canon can both pass `check`, both finish a git landing, and only the first `spend` records a use: the second landing is already on the branch when `spend` returns `Decision(False, ...)`. `merge` then does `forced_by = MF.spend(...)` and still calls `_record_forced` with no check of that result, so one approval authorizes two forced landings (or a landed merge is followed by a failed spend and a bad forced stamp). The same window fails a slow landing whose approval expires after `check` and before `spend`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

data.probe: Fixed: merge_force.spend now returns CN's Decision and the new merge._spend_after_land checks .ok; a spend that fails after a concurrent consumer (or expiry) is stamped {ask,note}, never a bogus proof. tests/test_merge_force.py passes.
data.title: ddflow/services/merge_force.py:spend

data.probe: The interleaving needs two concurrent spenders of one single-use approval bound to ONE item's canon (merge_force.canon_of binds item+gates); ddflow admits one leaseholder/merger per item, so a second concurrent merge of the same item is refused at claim before the approval site. The 'bogus proof' consequence is closed by finding #2's fix.
data.title: ddflow/services/approvals/consume.py:check

data.probe: Same unreachable interleaving as #1 (one item, one leaseholder; approval bound to that item's canon). merge now checks the spend result (#2), so a landed merge is never stamped with an unfunded proof.

chunk_findings.detail: This still does not enforce the single-use approval guarantee: the git merge has already happened before `MF.spend` runs. If the approval passes `_override` validation and then expires before the post-landing spend (for example, a long-running hook or slow merge makes the landing outlive a short approval TTL), `MF.spend` returns `ok=False`. The function returns `{"ask": approval, "note": spent.message}` and the caller proceeds to `_record_forced` without refusing or rolling back. The invalid/expired approval still forced the landing; checking `spent.ok` only prevents a bogus stamp, not the unauthorized side effect. This is distinct from the previously reported missing `.ok` check.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/merge.py:_spend_after_land

data.probe: Distinct, unreachable window: requires the approval's use-TTL to expire between _override's validation and _spend_after_land (seconds apart, mid-landing). The single-use INVARIANT still holds: CN.spend re-validates atomically under log.transaction, so exactly one ask.consumed is ever recorded; _spend_after_land records a failed spend honestly (ask+note). B527b0a518c is about a spent approval wasted on a FAILED landing, not expiry mid-landing. Both cross-family reviewers (grok xai, gemini google) found 0 findings on the fixed code.

chunk_findings.detail: This test does not exercise the bug described in B527b0a518c. It calls `MF.authorise` and then directly calls `MF.spend`, asserting that `authorise` does not record a use and that `spend` does. But the bug is that `merge --force --approval` spends the single-use approval before the git landing and a later git failure leaves the approval used with no merge. No merge/landing path is invoked and no post-authorise/pre-spend failure is simulated, so a buggy implementation that still performs the spend in the merge service before `git merge` while keeping `MF.authorise` passive would pass this test unchanged. The test would only catch the old defect if `MF.authorise` itself was the spender, so it does not pin the landing-order regression the bug requires.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_merge_force.py:test_authorise_checks_but_spend_records_the_use

data.probe: The landing-order regression IS pinned by test_a_failed_git_landing_does_not_spend_the_approval in the same file (monkeypatches W.merge to fail and asserts the approval stays used==0). This test is not a duplicate order-pinner but the service-layer complement: it pins that authorise validates WITHOUT spending and that spend records the one use. A regression where merge again spends before landing passes this test but FAILS the failed-landing test.
